---
title: "Figure 15.1: Effect of 2025 US Tariffs on China on LAC Imports from China"
---

![Python: `python/fig-15-1.py`](../images/python/fig-15-1.png)

The predicted change in imports from China for four countries, as a result
of the 2025 US tariffs on China. The idea is trade diversion: when Chinese
goods face higher tariffs in the United States, some of them are sold in
Latin America instead. One bar per country, all positive.

**The simplest bar chart in the set.** If you want to make a new bar chart,
this script is the template to start from.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 4 rows:

| category | series_0 |
|---|---|
| Mexico | 7.5 |
| ... | |

The single series has no name in Excel, so it is called `series_0`. The
extraction step gives every unnamed series a name of this form (`series_0`,
`series_1`, ...), numbered in the order of the series in the Excel chart.
Since there is no legend, the name never appears in the chart.

## The script

The whole script, apart from the imports and the texts:

```python
data = read_chart_data(STEM)

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Effect of 2025 US Tariffs on China on LAC Imports\nfrom China",
    subtitle="(Predicted change in imports from China; percent)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Arizala, Schauer, and Grittayaphong (forthcoming); and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)

x = np.arange(len(data))
ax.bar(x, data["series_0"], width=0.56, color="#5B2875")

ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"])
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 8, 2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.8)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
```

What each step does:

1. **Reading the data.** `read_chart_data(STEM)` reads sheet `data` of
   `excel_and_png/fig-15-1.xlsx` into a pandas DataFrame, a table with named
   columns. See [Reading the data](../chart-style.qmd#sec-read).
2. **The frame.** `new_chart()` creates the 5 × 5 inch figure, writes the
   title, subtitle and sources, and returns the figure (`fig`) and the plot
   area (`ax`). The title is split where the published chart splits it,
   with `\n`. The caption is only two lines, so the plot is taller than in
   most charts. See [The frame](../chart-style.qmd#sec-new-chart).
3. **Positions.** The country names are text, and bars need numeric
   x-positions. `np.arange(len(data))` gives 0, 1, 2, 3, one per country.
   See [Categories as positions](../techniques.qmd#sec-categories).
4. **The bars.** `ax.bar(x, heights, width=..., color=...)` draws one bar at
   each position, as high as the value in `series_0`. `width=0.56` means
   each bar takes 56 percent of the space per category, which leaves a gap
   of 44 percent between bars. In Excel's terms that is a *gap width* of
   about 80 percent (0.44 / 0.56). The colour `#5B2875` is the REO's dark
   purple.
5. **The labels.** `ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"])` puts the country
   names under the bars. `length=0` hides the tick marks, as Excel does for
   a bar chart's category axis, and `pad=5` leaves a little space between
   the axis and the names.
6. **The x-limits.** `ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)` runs from half a
   step before the first bar to half a step after the last. Each bar is
   then centred in an equal slice of the width, as in Excel.
7. **The y-axis** runs from 0 to 8, with ticks every 2 pointing in. The
   shared helper `set_y_scale()` sets the limits and the ticks in one call.
   See [The y-scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-y-scale).
8. **Saving.** `save_chart(fig, STEM)` writes
   `python/figures/fig-15-1.png` at 600 dpi.

## Changing the chart

Because the script is so short, most changes are one line:

- **Value labels on the bars.** Keep what `ax.bar()` returns and pass it to
  `ax.bar_label()`:

  ```python
  bars = ax.bar(x, data["series_0"], width=0.56, color="#5B2875")
  ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f", padding=2)
  ```

- **Negative values.** If some bars go below zero, change the y-scale, for
  example `set_y_scale(ax, -2, 8, 2)`, and add a line at zero with
  `ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.6)`. See [An axis line at
  zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).
- **Horizontal bars.** Use `ax.barh(x, data["series_0"], height=0.56, ...)`
  and `ax.set_yticks(x, data["category"])`. Remember that the y-axis counts
  upwards, so the first country is at the bottom; `ax.invert_yaxis()` puts
  it at the top.
- **More countries.** Nothing has to change: `len(data)` adjusts the
  positions and limits. With long names, add `rotation=90` to
  `set_xticks()` and increase `bottom_gap`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-15-1.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-15-1.py"}
"""Figure 15.1: Effect of 2025 US Tariffs on China on LAC Imports from China."""
import numpy as np

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-15-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Effect of 2025 US Tariffs on China on LAC Imports\nfrom China",
    subtitle="(Predicted change in imports from China; percent)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Arizala, Schauer, and Grittayaphong (forthcoming); and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)

x = np.arange(len(data))
ax.bar(x, data["series_0"], width=0.56, color="#5B2875")

ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"])
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 8, 2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.8)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
